newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling weakens, flights delayed, diverted.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling weakens, flights delayed, diverted.

text.p: Pressures on Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi's government grew on Monday as an air traffic controllers' go-slow brought chaos to tourist flights and the currency weakened further against the dollar.
The third day of the protest by controllers delayed passenger and cargo flights for up to 12 hours in the high season for one of Africa's main tourist destinations.

The Kenyan shilling's international value slid further on Monday with high dollar demand after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a $205 million aid package on Thursday because of high-level corruption.
"The go-slow is in its third day and it is absolute chaos out there," said an air traffic controller at Kenyatta Airport.

An official at national carrier Kenya Airways said planes leaving Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta airport were delayed by between three and 12 hours and arriving flights were waiting up to two hours to land in Kenya.
"We are moving to crisis point. We hope the government will intervene to resolve the issue," the airline official added.
But officials said formal talks between the controllers and the government had not yet begun despite complaints from tourists, airlines and businesses.
Jomo Kenyatta is the main cargo and passenger hub for East Africa and for some air cargo carriers is even more important than airports in South Africa, the continent's economic leader.
The industrial action is hitting other Kenyan airports at Mombasa, Kisumu and Malindi.
Air traffic controllers who say they earn about $90 a month began a go-slow at midnight on Friday, demanding a 50-fold pay increase, housing allowances and government-backed mortgages.
Meteorologists who supply weather information have launched a go-slow, increasing problems in flying in all of East Africa.
Lufthansa Cargo said most of its Frankfurt-bound perishable cargo at the weekend was delayed more than 24 hours because late departures from Nairobi meant most connections were missed.

Airlink said it stood to lose completely a cargo of five tonnes of fresh flowers, awaiting a connection to South Africa since Saturday. Tourism is Kenya's biggest hard currency earner with flowers and fresh produce in fourth place.
Ironically, Kenyan exporters led by flower growers and tourism companies have pressed since 1994 for a weaker shilling, saying its previous strong value made them uncompetitive.
The go-slow struck as the Moi government was squeezed over corruption and political reforms.
The shilling opened at 62.50 to the dollar, from Friday's close of 61, and it later weakened to nearly 63, three percent down from Friday's close, according to commercial bank rates.
There was no activity on the foreign board at the Nairobi Stock Exchange and foreign investors offloaded Central Bank of Kenya floating-rate treasury bonds.
Moi, 73 and Kenya's ruler for 19 years, hit out on Sunday at the IMF decision to cancel the loan, saying the reasons were political and ordinary Kenyans would be hurt.
An alliance of opposition-backed groups pressing the government for political reforms before a general election later this year has called for a national general strike on Friday.
Labour Minister Philip Masinde declared the strike illegal on Sunday and said those who stayed away from work would not be protected from employers' sanctions.
Six trade unions said they should have been consulted on the general strike call and told workers to ignore it.
The government said on Friday it would raise revenues and cut spending to cover some of the $215 million loss this year as it could not count on aid from the IMF and other multilateral donors.
